questions.prompt: Why must you always call the `cancel` function returned by WithCancel/WithTimeout?

options.text: To release the resources (timers, goroutines) the context set up
It is optional and has no effect
To send the result to the caller

questions.explanation: Not calling cancel leaks the context's resources until the deadline; `defer cancel()` is the idiom, and go vet warns when you forget.

questions.prompt: How does a function learn that a context has been cancelled or timed out?

options.text: The channel from ctx.Done() is closed; ctx.Err() says why

questions.explanation: ctx.Done() returns a channel that closes on cancellation/timeout; ctx.Err() then returns context.Canceled or context.DeadlineExceeded.

questions.prompt: By convention, a Context is passed as the ____ parameter of a function, named ctx.
questions.explanation: Pass ctx as the first argument named ctx; don't store it in a struct.

options.text: Request-scoped data crossing API boundaries, with an unexported key type

questions.explanation: WithValue is for request-scoped data (like a request ID) across boundaries, using an unexported key type to avoid collisions — not for normal parameters.

questions.prompt: Which are correct context practices? Select all that apply.

options.text: Derive a timeout at a boundary and defer cancel() immediately
Select on ctx.Done() in long loops so work can be cancelled
Propagate the same context down the call chain
Store the Context in a struct field for later use

questions.explanation: Derive-and-defer-cancel, watch ctx.Done(), and propagate the context are all correct. Storing a context in a struct is discouraged.

questions.prompt: Match each context constructor to its role.

pairs.right: A placeholder when none is wired yet
Manual cancellation via a cancel func

questions.explanation: Background is the root, TODO is a placeholder, WithTimeout bounds time, and WithCancel gives manual cancellation.
